before.content_html:
Why This Battlefield Matters

The Battle of Hastings is your specified site for the 2027 exam. That means Paper 2 will ask you a 16-mark question that names the battlefield, with four further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. It asks for something specific: not just the story of the battle, but how the place — the ridge, the slopes, the marshy ground — shaped what happened on it. This lesson gives you the battle through the lens of its environment. The narrative background is in Lesson 2; here we walk the ground.

Why the Armies Met Seven Miles from Hastings

The battle of 14 October 1066 was not fought at Hastings at all, but on a ridge about seven miles to the north-west, where the town of Battle now stands. Geography put both commanders there. William had landed at Pevensey and moved to Hastings, a port on a narrow peninsula of land — easy to defend, easy to supply by sea, but also easy to bottle up. He could not sit there through the winter, so he burned and plundered the surrounding villages to force a quick fight. Harold, marching south at speed after his victory at Stamford Bridge, took the bait — this was his own family heartland being harried. He halted his army across the London road, on a ridge blocking the only good route out of the Hastings peninsula.

Key Fact

The battlefield sits on a ridge seven miles north-west of Hastings, across the London road — the route William had to take to break out of his peninsula. The town of Battle grew up on the site afterwards. Some chroniclers called the ridge Senlac Hill.

Reading the Ground: Ridge, Slope and Marsh

Harold’s position was chosen with a soldier’s eye. His army formed up along the crest of the ridge, roughly seven hundred metres wide — about the frontage his men could fill standing shoulder to shoulder. In front of them the ground fell away, steeply in places, towards the low ground where William’s army would have to form up beneath them. On either flank the slopes dropped into small stream valleys with soft, marshy ground, which protected the English from being outflanked. Behind the ridge lay the forest of the Weald, cover for a retreat if one was needed. An attacker had one realistic option: come straight up the hill.

That suited Harold exactly, because his army had no cavalry and few archers. English warfare was infantry warfare: his elite housecarls and the part-time soldiers of the fyrd fought on foot in a shield wall. A shield wall on a hilltop with protected flanks was the strongest thing an Anglo-Saxon army could build. As long as it held its ground, it was very hard to break.

The Armies on the Field

Historians estimate perhaps seven thousand men on each side. Harold’s were all infantry — housecarls in the front ranks with their two-handed axes, fyrdmen packed behind. William’s army was a combined-arms force in three divisions: Bretons on his left, Normans in his centre, French and Flemish troops on his right. Each division layered archers in front, armoured infantry behind them, and mounted knights at the rear. That mix — missiles, foot and cavalry working together — was the Norman way of war, and the whole battle turned on whether the ground would let it work.

William’s army was living off a small, stripped peninsula as autumn closed in. Disease was the great killer of invading armies, his ships were vulnerable to October storms, and every week of delay let Harold gather more men. Provoking a battle quickly was not aggression for its own sake — it was the only plan that worked. It is also why the battlefield is where it is: William marched out to fight the moment his scouts reported Harold’s arrival, before the English position could strengthen further.

How the Environment Shaped the Fighting

The battle began in the morning and lasted until dusk — extraordinary for a medieval battle, which was usually decided in an hour or two. The length of the fight is itself evidence of what the ground did. Norman arrows, shot uphill, thudded into shields or sailed over the ridge. Norman knights charging uphill arrived at the shield wall slow and winded, and the wall held. Attack after attack rolled up the slope and broke.

The environment also produced the battle’s great crisis. On the Norman left, the Bretons — fighting on the lowest, softest ground near the marshy stream — buckled and fled, and a rumour ran through the army that William was dead. Part of the English right charged down off the ridge in pursuit. William pushed back his helmet to show his face and rallied his knights, who wheeled round and cut down the pursuers on the low ground, away from the wall’s protection. Chroniclers say the Normans then used feigned retreats to repeat the trick on purpose. Every man tempted downhill was a brick pulled out of the wall.

Key Fact

The battle lasted from morning until dusk — far longer than most medieval battles. The ridge is the reason: as long as the shield wall stayed on the crest with its flanks covered by marsh, Norman cavalry, archers and infantry could not combine effectively against it.

The End: The Ridge Breaks

By late afternoon the arithmetic of attrition was telling. The wall was thinner; tired fyrdmen stood where housecarls had fallen; Harold’s brothers Gyrth and Leofwine were already dead. William’s archers kept shooting, his knights kept probing, and at last the line gave. Harold fell — killed, in the famous tradition shown in the Bayeux Tapestry, by an arrow in the eye, though historians still debate exactly how he died. With the king dead the army broke into the Weald behind the ridge. Even the pursuit carried the stamp of the ground: chroniclers describe Norman horsemen in the dark tumbling into a steep hidden ditch — the Malfosse — where fleeing Englishmen turned and killed them.

The Site Afterwards: Battle Abbey

The battlefield’s history did not end at dusk. The Pope had backed William’s invasion, but the Church still demanded penance for the bloodshed, and William’s answer was built in stone: Battle Abbey, founded on the field itself, with the high altar placed — tradition says on William’s own orders — on the spot where Harold fell. The abbey terraced the ridge and a town grew at its gates, so today’s visitor sees a landscape partly reshaped by the monument to the battle. The site is in the care of English Heritage, and the surviving ridge, slopes and low ground are exactly the features your exam question is about.

Using the Site in the 16-Mark Question

The question will give you a statement and ask how far a study of the battlefield supports it. The skill is pairing a physical feature with a consequence: the crest explains why the shield wall held all day; the marshy flanks explain why William had to attack frontally; the slope explains why cavalry and arrows underperformed; the low ground explains why leaving the wall was fatal; and the site’s position astride the London road explains why the battle happened here at all. Site feature, then consequence, then link to the statement — that chain is what earns the marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the ground Harold chose for the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The ridge: the English position ran along a crest roughly seven hundred metres wide, forcing any attacker to advance uphill, which slowed cavalry and reduced the effect of archery.
• The marshy flanks: small stream valleys with soft ground on either side of the ridge prevented the Normans outflanking the shield wall.
• The London road: the site sat astride the main route out of the Hastings peninsula, which is why Harold chose it to block William's advance.
• The Weald: forest behind the ridge offered the English cover for retreat and later hid the Malfosse ditch.
• Why it mattered: the ridge, the marshy flanks and the London road together forced William into frontal uphill attacks, which is why an all-infantry army held out until dusk.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of the English defeat.

‘Harold picked the strongest position in England and his shield wall was unbeatable on it. The English lost Hastings only because their own men would not stay on the ridge.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons for the English defeat at Hastings? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: the position was so strong that only English indiscipline can explain the defeat.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The shield wall held the crest against archers, infantry and cavalry from morning until late afternoon, which was extraordinary for a medieval battle.
• Marshy stream valleys on both flanks stopped William outflanking the line, so every attack had to come uphill.
• Part of the English right left the crest to chase the fleeing Bretons and was cut down on the low ground; the feigned retreats then repeated the trick.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• The wall was already thinning through attrition, and the fyrd was standing where housecarls had fallen; discipline was not the only pressure on it.
• Harold’s army was worn down by Stamford Bridge and a fast march, and he chose to fight before all his men had arrived.
• William’s handling of the crisis — riding bare-headed to rally the line, then using the retreats deliberately — was skill, not English error alone.
• Harold’s death, and those of Gyrth and Leofwine, removed the leadership that held the line together.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about Harold’s choice of ground at the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the crest, slopes and marshy flanks made the all-infantry English army as strong as it could be, forcing frontal uphill attacks that failed from morning to late afternoon.
• Strategically: by planting his army on the London road, Harold turned a battle into the decisive engagement — William had to win here or starve in his peninsula.
• Limits of the choice: the position could hold but not manoeuvre; once discipline slipped and men followed the fleeing Bretons downhill, the same slopes became a killing ground, showing the choice of ground only worked while the wall held it.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the way the battlefield environment shaped the fighting at Hastings on 14 October 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Morning: Normans form up on the low ground and attack uphill; arrows shot uphill are wasted against shields; charges arrive winded and the wall holds.
• The crisis: the Bretons on the softest ground near the marsh break and flee; the rumour that William is dead; William lifts his helmet to rally his men; English pursuers are destroyed on the low ground.
• Afternoon: feigned retreats repeatedly tempt men off the crest; attrition thins the wall through a battle of exceptional length.
• Dusk: the wall finally breaks, Harold is killed, and even the pursuit is shaped by the ground at the Malfosse ditch.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the death of King Harold at the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: the shield wall had held all day while he lived; his death (with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine already dead) removed all leadership and the army broke.
• Politically: there was no adult, crowned rival left with comparable legitimacy — the battle became a conquest of the whole kingdom rather than one lost battle.
• For the site: tradition places the high altar of Battle Abbey on the spot where he fell, showing how the Normans themselves marked his death as the decisive moment.
• The debated manner of death (the Bayeux Tapestry arrow tradition) shows how quickly the event passed into propaganda and legend.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: 'William won the Battle of Hastings because of his enemies' mistakes rather than his own skill.' How far does a study of the battlefield at Hastings support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the battlefield and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• English troops abandoned the crest to pursue the Bretons and were destroyed on the low ground — the site shows discipline failing, since the position was only strong while held.
• Harold offered battle before his army was complete, fresh from the Stamford Bridge campaign, when waiting would have strengthened him and starved William.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• William's combined-arms coordination on unfavourable ground — rotating archers, infantry and cavalry against a hilltop wall for a whole day — was skill, not luck.
• The rally after the Breton collapse (the helmet moment) and the disciplined use of feigned retreats turned the terrain's one weakness for the defenders into a weapon.
• The campaign context: harrying Harold's family lands to force battle at a time of William's choosing was calculated generalship.
A developed judgement weighing site evidence against contextual knowledge is required for the top level.

[16 marks, plus 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar]
Mastering: A sustained judgement, built from named features of the site and tested against wider knowledge of the period.
Secure: Clear argument using site features and relevant contextual knowledge.
Developing: Some use of the site, with limited wider knowledge.
Emerging: Describes the site without answering the statement.

before.content_html:
A Building That Is Also an Argument

The White Tower is your specified site for the 2028 exam. Unlike a battlefield, this site is a single building you can still walk through — and the 16-mark question (with 4 further marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar) rewards you for reading it like a document. Every feature of the Tower makes a claim about Norman power: where it stands, what it is made of, how you get in, and what William wanted the largest city in his new kingdom to feel every time it looked up. Lesson 7 gave you castles as a system; this lesson reads one building in depth.

Why There, Why Then

London was not conquered at Hastings. The city — by far the biggest and richest in England — submitted to William by negotiation in late 1066, and a city that chooses to submit can choose to change its mind. William’s answer was to build castles inside it. Immediately after his coronation he ordered fortifications in the city’s south-east corner, and around the mid-1070s work began there on something new in England: a colossal stone keep. The site was chosen with precision. It sat in the angle of the surviving Roman city walls, which protected two of its sides and let the builders work securely inside a defended corner — and it commanded the Thames, the river road by which trade, tribute and any hostile fleet would come.

Key Fact

Work on the great stone keep began around the mid-1070s under William I, supervised by Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester, a churchman famed as a builder. It was substantially complete by around 1100. The name ‘White Tower’ came later, when the walls were whitewashed in the thirteenth century.

Reading the Building: Stone, Height and Thickness

The Tower’s fabric is itself evidence. Much of the stone is Kentish ragstone, but the dressings — the sharp corners and window surrounds — are fine pale limestone shipped across the Channel from Caen in Normandy. Importing stone by sea was staggeringly expensive; William did it anyway, because the building was meant to look Norman, to be visibly made of the conquerors’ own land. The keep rose roughly ninety feet, with walls up to fifteen feet thick at the base, corner turrets above the roofline, and small, high windows. In a city of timber and thatch, nothing remotely like it existed. Chroniclers and townsmen alike understood the message: this building was not going away, and neither were its owners.

Compare it with Lesson 7’s motte-and-bailey castles and the difference in purpose is obvious. An earth-and-timber castle was fast war-time architecture — up in a fortnight, disposable. The White Tower took a generation to build. It was permanence made of stone: the conquest declaring itself finished.

Reading the Building: How You Get In

The entrance tells its own story. The door stood at first-floor level, reached by an external wooden stair that could be removed in a crisis, leaving attackers facing fifteen feet of blank wall. Inside, the keep stacked its functions vertically: storage in the basement, garrison and business below, and above them the great hall and chambers where the king or his constable lived, held court and overawed visitors. The building was simultaneously a fortress, a palace, a treasury and a prison — the whole apparatus of Norman lordship under one roof.

Built into the keep’s south-east corner is the Chapel of St John the Evangelist — a complete Norman church of massive round arches, in Caen stone, inside a fortress. It is one of the best-preserved early Norman interiors anywhere, and it matters for your exam because it joins two of your themes in one room: the same regime that built castles also rebuilt the English Church (Lesson 11), and at the White Tower it did both in the same building.

One Tower Among Three

The White Tower did not control London alone. Two lesser castles — Baynard’s Castle and Montfichet’s Tower — were planted at the city’s western end, so that Norman garrisons bracketed London from both sides. That pattern repeats what you saw across the kingdom: York got two castles; strategic towns got theirs driven through demolished houses. The difference at the Tower is scale and material. London was the prize of the kingdom, so it received the statement building — the keep that out-built anything the English had ever seen.

Key Fact

Baynard’s Castle and Montfichet’s Tower stood at London’s western end, bracketing the city with the White Tower in the east — the standard Norman pattern of controlling towns from multiple strongpoints, applied to the greatest town of all.

What the Site Shows About Norman England

Pull the features together and the Tower becomes a summary of the whole conquest. The location shows the Normans’ priorities: London and its river first. The Roman walls show their practicality: build where the ground already defends you. The Caen stone shows identity and expense deployed as propaganda. The first-floor door and fifteen-foot walls show a ruling minority that expected rebellion — this was built during the years of revolt you studied in Lessons 4 and 5. The chapel shows Church and Crown fused. And the sheer scale shows the ambition that separates William’s conquest from a mere raid: he was building for centuries.

The Site Afterwards and in the Exam

The keep still stands at the heart of the Tower of London, wrapped in the walls later kings added, and the fortress around it has served as armoury, prison, mint and menagerie since. For the 16-mark question, work feature by feature and attach each to a purpose: Caen stone → Norman identity displayed; first-floor entrance → security against a hostile city; position on the Thames and Roman walls → control of trade and approach; scale in stone → permanence aimed at Londoners’ minds as much as their walls. Feature, purpose, consequence — then weigh it against your wider knowledge of how the Normans held England.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the design of the White Tower.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A colossal stone keep roughly ninety feet tall with walls up to fifteen feet thick at the base, corner turrets and small high windows.
• Caen limestone dressings imported by sea from Normandy, over Kentish ragstone walling — Norman identity built into the fabric.
• A first-floor entrance reached by a removable external stair, leaving attackers facing blank wall.
• The Chapel of St John the Evangelist built into the keep — a complete Norman church inside the fortress.
• Its position in the angle of the Roman city walls, commanding the Thames approach to London.
• Why it mattered: height, thickness and a first-floor door told Londoners that a small Norman garrison could hold the city against them, and would.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation A: an interpretation written for this exercise. It sums up one view of Norman London.

‘London was never really conquered in 1066. It bargained, and the castles William planted in it show that he knew a city that submits by choice can change its mind.’

How convincing is Interpretation A about Norman control of London after 1066? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — How Convincing Is the Interpretation
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• What the interpretation says: London submitted by negotiation rather than conquest, and the Norman castles there were built against that risk.

Knowledge that supports the interpretation:
• The city was not taken by assault: William circled it, ravaged the surrounding shires, and its leaders came out to submit at Berkhamsted.
• Fortifications went up in the city’s south-east corner immediately after the coronation, before any revolt had begun.
• Baynard’s Castle and Montfichet’s Tower were planted at the western end, so garrisons bracketed the city from both sides.
• The keep faced inwards as much as outwards: a first-floor entrance up a removable stair and walls fifteen feet thick assume a hostile population close by.

Knowledge that challenges the interpretation:
• The Roman wall corner and the command of the Thames show the site was also chosen against attack from outside, including a Danish fleet.
• The keep was a palace and treasury as well as a fortress, so it was built for government, not only for fear.
• Two castles in one town was the standard Norman pattern at York and Lincoln too; London was not a special case of distrust.
• The building took a generation and was finished around 1100, long after the danger of a London rising had passed.

Judgement: say how far the interpretation is convincing, using both sides of the evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, tested against precise contextual knowledge, with a clear judgement on how convincing it is.
Secure: Clear evaluation supported by relevant knowledge.
Developing: Some comment on the interpretation with limited support.
Emerging: Describes the interpretation without judging it.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the building materials used in the White Tower.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stone itself was the message: against England's timber castles and houses, a ninety-foot stone keep declared permanence — the conquest was not a raid.
• Caen limestone, shipped at great expense from Normandy, made the building visibly Norman — identity and reach displayed in the fabric.
• The cost and the generation-long build show the resources the Norman state could command, including English labour and taxation.
• Durability had practical significance too: the keep resisted fire and assault in ways timber could not, and it still stands — evidence of intent fulfilled.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of how the Normans took control of London after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Late 1066: London submits by negotiation after William's army circles and devastates the surrounding counties; coronation at Westminster on Christmas Day.
• Immediately after: William orders fortifications in the city's south-east corner while he withdraws to Barking — castles inside the city from the start.
• Around the mid-1070s: work begins on the great stone keep under Gundulf of Rochester, protected by the Roman wall angle, commanding the Thames.
• The finished system: the White Tower in the east with Baynard's Castle and Montfichet's Tower in the west, garrisons bracketing England's greatest city.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain what was important about the White Tower for Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Control of London: the keep overawed the kingdom's largest, richest and most independent-minded city and commanded its river.
• Symbolically: scale, stone and Caen dressings made Norman permanence visible to every Londoner — psychological control alongside military.
• For government: fortress, palace, treasury and prison in one — royal government concentrated in a defensible point.
• Wider pattern: the Tower is the maximum case of the urban castle policy applied at York, Lincoln, Norwich and elsewhere — one building standing for a national system.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Two developed points on why this mattered, each supported with precise detail.
Secure: Two points on importance with relevant support.
Developing: One developed point, or two points with little support.
Emerging: Describes the topic without explaining why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: 'The White Tower was built to impress rather than to defend.' How far does a study of the White Tower support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the White Tower and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The expense of Caen stone and the sheer scale exceed any defensive need — a plain keep would defend as well; this one was designed to be seen and understood.
• The chapel, hall and royal chambers show a palace of lordship and ceremony, not a pure fortress.
• By the time the keep was substantially complete (c.1100), the era of great revolts was over — its finished role was statement more than shield.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• Fifteen-foot walls, the first-floor entrance with removable stair, small high windows and the Roman-wall corner are serious defensive engineering, designed while rebellion was live (1067-71).
• A garrison inside a hostile city genuinely needed a secure base — the Tower was to control London, and control needed both fear and physical security.
• The two functions were one Norman idea: a building that could not be taken WAS the impression.
A developed judgement weighing display against defence, tied to named features, is required for the top level.

[16 marks, plus 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar]
Mastering: A sustained judgement, built from named features of the site and tested against wider knowledge of the period.
Secure: Clear argument using site features and relevant contextual knowledge.
Developing: Some use of the site, with limited wider knowledge.
Emerging: Describes the site without answering the statement.
